fleetMemory.text: A lease taken once is a lease held only for the first batch, and the failure mode is worse than it sounds: with batched writes the OLD code did not 'write the second batch after expiry' — with no lease call between the take and the release, there was NO refusal anywhere in the middle of the run. The stolen-lease falsifier surfaced only out of the run's own RELEASE, after every batch had been written and journalled. When auditing any writer that takes a lease, grep for the lease call sites in the WRITE LOOP, not just at the top and bottom of the function; a take-then-release pair reads like a lease is held throughout, and structurally it is held at neither end of the middle.

Put the heartbeat on the SAME transaction as the writes it protects, as the FIRST statement of that transaction. On a separate connection the extension can commit while the batch aborts (a window claimed for work that never happened) or the batch can commit while the extension rolls back (a write under an expiry nobody advanced). It also has to come BEFORE the journal insert, so a lost lease cannot leave a journal row describing a batch that was then refused: journal-then-write is the 'no record, no write' order, and the heartbeat sits ahead of both.

`pnpm typecheck` in this repo typechecks `src` only — every package's tsconfig has `include: ["src"]`, so `packages/engine-core/scripts/*.mts` (the apply, the census, the classifier, the guards) is covered by NOTHING in CI, and an ad-hoc `tsc` over such a script reports a wall of pre-existing implicit-any errors that are noise rather than signal. The real gate for script-layer code is the tests that run it plus the repo's own typecheck for the `src` it imports. Do not read 'typecheck clean' as a statement about a script.

Do NOT try to prove a lease heartbeat by sleeping past the TTL in a test. 15 minutes is the TTL and the suite would be unusable; drive the clock instead (the cores accept an injected `now`). For the STOLEN case a one-shot fixture trigger on the written table is what makes the theft happen at a batch boundary the test controls, rather than at a time it hopes for. Also do not try to distinguish 'same transaction' from 'same connection' with a driven clock — that property can only be READ, and it is honest to label it a reading.

Do NOT add a lease guard by RE-TAKING the scope per batch. `takeScopedLease` steals an expired scope, so a re-take on the run path would let this writer take a county from a live holder mid-run — a worse defect than the one being fixed. `lockAndHeartbeatLease` extends THIS holder token's row and never re-takes; keeping exactly one take on the run path is what makes 'the scope is normally free' true rather than a claim. Note also that `releaseScopedLease` DELETEs by holder token, which is why a release after a theft cannot remove the thief's row.
